country.name: South Africa
country.summary: South Africa's wine country is the Western Cape, a narrow band of mountain valleys within reach of two oceans at the foot of Africa. The industry dates from 1659, when the first Cape wine was pressed at the Dutch supply station, and it was reborn after 1994, when the end of sanctions opened the export markets. Chenin Blanc, long called Steen, is the most planted grape, and the country holds more of it than France. Cabernet Sauvignon leads the reds, Pinotage is the home crossing of 1925, and Syrah carries the Swartland's reputation. The Wine of Origin scheme of 1973 certifies where the grapes grew, the vintage and the variety, and says nothing about style. Bottle-fermented sparkling wine is Cap Classique, and the sweet Muscat of Constantia is the oldest famous wine of the southern hemisphere.
country.overview:
The Cape was planted to supply ships, not to make fine wine. The Dutch East India Company's station at Table Bay planted vines in 1655 and pressed its first wine on 2 February 1659. Simon van der Stel, the governor who founded Stellenbosch in 1679, took the Constantia land in 1685, and the Huguenots who arrived from 1688 settled the valley that became Franschhoek. Constantia's sweet Muscat was the Cape's one wine of world renown through the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Then came phylloxera in 1886, overproduction, and in 1918 the KWV, the growers' co-operative at Paarl, which fixed prices and from 1957 a quota on planting. Fortified wine and brandy ruled for most of the twentieth century. The Wine of Origin scheme arrived in 1973, Pinotage had been crossed in 1925, and bottle-fermented sparkling wine was first made at Stellenbosch in 1971. Isolation ended with the 1994 election, exports grew many times over, and the old vineyard has been rethought twice since: by the Swartland growers who turned dry-farmed bush vines into fine wine from about 2000, and by the Old Vine Project, whose Certified Heritage Vineyard seal from 2018 prints the planting date of a vineyard of thirty five years or more.

The geography is the Cape Fold Belt. Ancient Malmesbury shale lies at the base, Cape granite pushed up through it as rounded plutons such as the Paardeberg and Paarl Mountain and lies under the foot slopes of the Simonsberg, and Table Mountain sandstone caps the high ridges. The climate is Mediterranean, with winter rain and a dry ripening season, cooled not by latitude but by water: the cold Benguela current up the Atlantic side, the warmer Indian Ocean across False Bay and Walker Bay, and the Cape Doctor, the dry summer south-easter that keeps canopies free of rot. Cool sites come from the sea, at Constantia, Walker Bay and Elim, or from height, at Elgin.

The Wine of Origin scheme nests four tiers inward: geographical unit (Western Cape), region (Coastal Region, Breede River Valley, Cape South Coast, Olifants River, Klein Karoo), district (Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland, Franschhoek Valley, Robertson, Walker Bay) and ward (Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Constantia). A stated origin must be true for every grape in the bottle; a stated vintage or variety for 85 per cent. Nothing in the scheme tells a grower what to plant or how to make wine. Estate Wine is grown, made and bottled on one registered unit, and a single vineyard is a registered block of one variety of no more than six hectares. The numbered seal on the neck has, since 2010, also certified the farm's sustainability programme.

The exam leans on a short list: Chenin Blanc as Steen and the scale of its plantings, Pinotage's parents, Stellenbosch for Cabernet and Bordeaux blends, the Swartland for Syrah and old-vine Chenin, Walker Bay and the Hemel-en-Aarde for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Constantia for Vin de Constance, Robertson for Chardonnay and Cap Classique, and the Wine of Origin percentages.
ladder: The broadest Wine of Origin tier: the Western Cape holds nearly the whole vineyard; the Northern Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo are among the others.
A grouping of districts: Coastal Region, Breede River Valley, Cape South Coast, Olifants River and Klein Karoo; Boberg is a region name reserved for fortified wine from the Paarl and Tulbagh country.
The working appellation a server names: Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland, Franschhoek Valley, Robertson, Walker Bay, Elgin, Darling, Wellington, Cape Town.
The smallest tier, a named locality of shared soil and climate inside or outside a district: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Constantia, Elim.
Grapes grown, wine made and bottled on one registered production unit; a label term since the rules of the mid 2000s replaced the old estate registration.
A registered vineyard of one variety, no larger than six hectares, named on the label.

The numbered seal of the Wine and Spirit Board guarantees stated origin, vintage and variety after analysis and tasting; since 2010 it is the Integrity and Sustainability seal, with the farm's sustainability audit folded in.
The Old Vine Project's seal, from 2018, for wine from a vineyard of thirty five years or more, carrying the planting date on the bottle.
labels: Wine of Origin, Wyn van Oorsprong
The certified origin statement; WO on an English label.
Steen
The old Cape name for Chenin Blanc.
Stein
An old term for a semi-sweet white style, not a grape; a false friend of Steen.
Hanepoot
Muscat of Alexandria, used for sweet, fortified and table wine.
Hermitage
The Cape's old name for Cinsaut, the second parent of Pinotage.
Groendruif
The old name for Sémillon, once the Cape's dominant grape.
Cape Riesling
Crouchen Blanc, not Riesling; true Riesling was long sold as Weisser or Rhine Riesling.
Cap Classique
Sparkling wine with its second fermentation in the bottle it is sold in; the trade's older form was Méthode Cap Classique, MCC.
Jerepigo, jerepiko
Grape juice fortified before fermentation starts, very sweet, often from Hanepoot.
Cape Vintage, Cape Tawny, Cape Ruby, Cape LBV
The port styles, named without the word port; Calitzdorp in the Klein Karoo is their home.
Noble Late Harvest
A botrytis-affected sweet wine; Late Harvest and Special Late Harvest are the lighter sweet categories beneath it.
Cape Blend
A red blend built on Pinotage; a trade term, not a legal one.
Landgoedwyn
Estate Wine in Afrikaans.
Vonkelwyn
Sparkling wine in Afrikaans, of any method.
Perlé
A lightly carbonated wine, well below sparkling pressure.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the country's calling card: everything from brisk, cheap dry white and brandy base to old bush-vine wines of quince, honey and beeswax, and botrytised dessert wine.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted red; firm, cedary, cassis-scented wines from Stellenbosch, often blended with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the Bordeaux manner.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Savoury, peppery, fynbos-scented wine from the Swartland's bush vines and fuller, riper Shiraz from Stellenbosch and Paarl.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Pungent, green-figgy and grassy from the cool coast and from Elgin, Constantia, Durbanville, Elim and Darling.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fine in the cool corners, Elgin and the Hemel-en-Aarde, on Robertson's lime-rich soils, and as the backbone of Cap Classique.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: The 1925 Stellenbosch crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut: smoky, plummy, mulberry-scented reds, rustic when rushed, and the core of the Cape Blend.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The softening partner in Stellenbosch Bordeaux blends and a plump varietal wine on the warmer sites.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: A perfumed, leafy component of the Cape's best blends, bottled alone by a few Stellenbosch houses.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: The old Hermitage of the Cape, once the workhorse red, now revived from old vines as a pale, fragrant, lightly chilled red.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Fine, savoury, red-fruited wine from the Hemel-en-Aarde and Elgin, the Cape's two Burgundian corners.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: A Swartland favourite for pale, spicy reds and for Rhône-style blends with Syrah and Cinsaut.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Groendruif, nine tenths of the Cape's vines in the 1820s, now a waxy, honeyed white from old Franschhoek vines and a partner to Sauvignon Blanc.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Muscat of Alexandria is Hanepoot, for sweet and fortified wine; Muscat de Frontignan, the small-berried Muscat, makes Vin de Constance.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.styles: A high-acid white for brandy and bulk wine along the Breede and Olifants rivers; rarely seen on a fine list.

exam: Chenin Blanc is Steen, the most planted grape, and South Africa holds more Chenin than France.
Pinotage: Pinot Noir crossed with Cinsaut at Stellenbosch in 1925, Cinsaut then called Hermitage, hence the name.
The Wine of Origin tiers and percentages: origin 100 per cent, vintage and variety 85 per cent, and no rule on style.

District to grape: Stellenbosch Cabernet and blends, Swartland Syrah and Chenin, Walker Bay Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Constantia Sauvignon Blanc and Vin de Constance, Robertson Chardonnay and Cap Classique, Elgin cool whites.
Cap Classique as the sparkling term, Estate Wine as grown, made and bottled on one unit, and a single vineyard at six hectares or less.
The map: the Coastal Region holds Stellenbosch, Paarl, Franschhoek, Swartland, Darling and Cape Town; the Breede River Valley holds Robertson; the Cape South Coast holds Elgin and Walker Bay.
The cooling agents: the Benguela current, False Bay, and the Cape Doctor south-easter.
traps: Steen is Chenin Blanc; Stein was a semi-sweet style. One letter, two meanings.
Hermitage on an old Cape label is Cinsaut, not Syrah, and Pinotage takes its second syllable from it.
Vin de Constance is not fortified; it is a late-picked, partly raisined Muscat de Frontignan, fermented and aged in wood.
Cape Riesling is Crouchen Blanc, and Hanepoot is Muscat of Alexandria, not the Muscat of Constantia.
Wine of Origin certifies place, vintage and grape; it never ranks a site or restricts a grape, so there is no grand cru and no grape list.
Hemel-en-Aarde is a valley in the Walker Bay district, not a brand, and Franschhoek is a district in its own right, no longer a ward of Paarl.
Constantia is a ward of the Cape Town district, and the Western Cape on a label is the geographical unit, the widest origin a fine wine normally carries.
Cap Classique is bottle fermented; Vonkelwyn is any sparkling wine and Perlé is merely fizzy.

The cold Benguela current on the Atlantic side, False Bay and Walker Bay on the south coast, altitude at Elgin, and the Cape Doctor, the dry summer south-easter.

cards.f: District to signature grape: six pairs
cards.b: Stellenbosch Cabernet; Swartland Syrah and old Chenin; Walker Bay Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Constantia Sauvignon Blanc and sweet Muscat; Robertson Chardonnay; Elgin cool whites.

cards.f: Three dates of Cape wine history
cards.b: 1659, the first wine pressed at the Cape; 1918, the KWV co-operative founded at Paarl; 1994, the election that reopened the export markets.

questions.q: Which two grapes were crossed at Stellenbosch in 1925 to make Pinotage?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir was crossed with Cinsaut, which the Cape then called Hermitage, so the new grape took the first syllables of both names. Syrah is the true grape of the Rhône's Hermitage hill, the source of the confusion.

questions.q: What is the traditional Cape name for Chenin Blanc?
questions.exp: Steen was the name used for Chenin Blanc for centuries; its identity with the Loire grape was confirmed in the 1960s. Stein, with an i, was an unrelated semi-sweet style.

questions.q: What share of a Wine of Origin certified wine must come from the vintage stated on the label?
questions.exp: A stated vintage, like a stated variety, must be true for 85 per cent of the wine. The stated origin alone must be true for every grape in the bottle, which is why candidates mix the two figures up.

questions.q: Which term names a South African sparkling wine whose second fermentation takes place in the bottle it is sold in?
questions.exp: Cap Classique, formerly Méthode Cap Classique, is the traditional method term. Vonkelwyn is Afrikaans for any sparkling wine, Perlé is lightly carbonated, and Noble Late Harvest is a botrytised sweet wine.

questions.q: In which year was South Africa's Wine of Origin scheme introduced?
questions.exp: The scheme came into force in 1973, giving the Cape a certified origin system decades before most of the New World.

questions.q: Which grape does the name Hanepoot stand for on a Cape label?
questions.exp: Hanepoot is Muscat of Alexandria, the grape of the Cape's sweet and fortified Muscats. The small-berried Muscat Blanc is the Constantia grape, and Crouchen Blanc hid for years as Cape Riesling.

questions.q: Which tier of the Wine of Origin scheme does Stellenbosch occupy?
questions.exp: Stellenbosch is a district within the Coastal Region, which sits within the Western Cape geographical unit; its own wards include Simonsberg-Stellenbosch and Jonkershoek Valley.

questions.q: Which Cape locality gave its name to the sweet Muscat that was the colony's one famous wine in the eighteenth century?
questions.exp: Simon van der Stel's Constantia estate of 1685 made the sweet Muscat de Frontignan that European courts bought; Klein Constantia revived it in the 1980s as Vin de Constance.

regions.name: Swartland
regions.summary: The Swartland is the hot, dry wheat country north of Cape Town, a district of the Coastal Region that was bulk wine land until a handful of growers showed, from about 2000, what its old dry-farmed bush vines could do. Its name means black land, after the renosterbos scrub that darkens the hills. Its wines are Syrah and Rhône-style red blends from the granite of the Paardeberg and the shale of the Riebeek hills, and Chenin Blanc from bush vines planted decades ago, savoury and textured. Malmesbury and Riebeek-Kasteel are the towns, Sadie Family Wines and Mullineux the houses the exam expects. Wine of Origin Swartland sets origin only; the growers' own charter of 2010 sets the style.

terroir.climate: Warm to hot Mediterranean, among the driest of the Cape districts: winter rain of roughly 300 to 500 millimetres, a long rainless summer and ripening days that pass 30 degrees. The Atlantic is near enough on the western side for afternoon breezes to reach the Paardeberg and the Darling hills, and nights cool sharply, which keeps acidity in grapes that have seen a great deal of sun.
terroir.soils: Two parents, read from any Swartland label. The Paardeberg is a dome of Cape granite that weathers to coarse, sandy, mineral-poor soil with pockets of clay; its wines are tense and perfumed. The Riebeek hills and the land around Malmesbury sit on Malmesbury shale and schist, which weather to heavier, iron-rich clay loams; their wines are deeper and more savoury. Porseleinberg's blue schist is the hardest and stoniest of all. Koffieklip, an iron-rich ferricrete gravel, turns up on both.
terroir.topography: Rolling wheat land between 100 and 300 metres, broken by three landmarks: the Paardeberg in the south on the Paarl border, the Kasteelberg above Riebeek-Kasteel and Riebeek West, and the Piketberg to the north. Vines take the slopes and the foot slopes of these hills, where the soil is poorer and the air moves; the plain between is grain and sheep.
terroir.water: The Berg River runs north through the district's eastern side on its way to the Atlantic at St Helena Bay, but most Swartland vineyards see no irrigation at all: the old bush vines are dry farmed on the winter rain their deep roots can find, and that habit is the district's identity.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The red that made the district's name: peppery, savoury, scented with fynbos and dried herb, firm but not heavy, fermented with whole bunches and aged in old wood, alone or leading a Rhône-style blend.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Old dry-farmed bush vines give concentrated, textured, honeyed whites with quince, straw and a saline finish, fermented in old barrels or concrete rather than new oak.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Pale, spicy and high-toned from bush vines on granite; a blending partner for Syrah and increasingly bottled alone.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Old vines of the Cape's Hermitage, revived for light, fragrant reds and as the lifting part of a red blend.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: Dark, meaty structure for the red blends, well suited to the heat.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Acid and bite from old vines, used sparingly in the red blends and occasionally bottled alone.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: Old bush-vine Pinotage made in a lighter, whole-bunch style, far from the heavy oaked wines of the 1990s.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot and perfume in the white blends, a small part beside Chenin, Clairette, Grenache Blanc and Roussanne.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.styles: Waxy weight and length in the Rhône-style white blends.

wines.note: Medium-bodied, dark-fruited and peppery, with dried herb, olive and a stony finish; firm tannin, little or no new oak. Serve at cellar temperature with lamb, duck or anything off the braai.
Syrah led, with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Cinsaut and Carignan in the southern Rhône manner; savoury, lifted and built to age. Columella is the wine the exam names.

Dry, full in texture, with quince, baked apple, honey and beeswax over bright acidity and a saline edge; a wine for roast chicken, pork belly and rich shellfish. Many carry the Certified Heritage Vineyard seal with a planting date.
Chenin Blanc with Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Viognier, Roussanne or Sémillon, fermented and aged in old oak or concrete; waxy, nutty, long and dry, the Cape's answer to a white Châteauneuf.
Pale, red-fruited, lightly chilled wines from old Cinsaut and Grenache, poured by the glass with charcuterie and spiced dishes.

wines.style: Cape port styles and Shiraz from the old estates
wines.note: The Riebeek West estates long made fortified wine from Portuguese varieties under the Cape Vintage and Cape Tawny names, alongside sturdy Shiraz; the older face of the district.

made.viticulture: The Swartland's claim rests on the bush vine, planted without wires and left to its own shade, dry farmed on winter rain. Many Chenin, Cinsaut, Grenache and Pinotage blocks date from the 1960s to the 1980s, and from 2018 the Old Vine Project's Certified Heritage Vineyard seal has let a producer print the planting date of any block of thirty five years or more. Yields are tiny, a few tonnes a hectare at best on the old blocks, because the vine sets what the moisture allows. Newer plantings of Syrah, Mourvèdre and the Rhône whites are often trellised, but the growers who set the style have kept to bush vines and to the poorest ground, the granite of the Paardeberg and the schist of the Riebeek and Porseleinberg hills. Harvest is early and fast, from late January, with the sugar watched closely because the heat can outrun the flavour; picking slightly early for freshness is the house habit. The hazards are drought, which in a dry year can halve a crop, wind and sunburn; rot is seldom a worry. The wheat land around is sprayed and ploughed, so the vineyard's own cover crops and organic or biodynamic farming matter here more than in most Cape districts.
made.winemaking: The district's winemaking is a manifesto as much as a method, written down in the charter of the Swartland Independent Producers in 2010: wine from Swartland fruit only, fermented with the vineyard's own yeasts, with no added acid, no added tannin and only a small share of new oak, so that the place shows rather than the cellar. Reds are fermented with a large portion of whole bunches, trodden or punched down by hand in open vats, concrete or old wood, with little extraction, and aged in old barrels, foudres or concrete eggs; blends are assembled late, in the manner of the southern Rhône. Whites are pressed whole bunch, fermented on their solids in old oak or concrete and left on the lees for months, which gives the waxy texture of the white blends. Chenin is kept dry and unoaked in flavour, even where it spent a year in wood. Skin-contact whites and pét-nat have a following in the district too, but the exam cares for the Syrah blends and the old-vine Chenin.

law.classification: Swartland is a Wine of Origin district within the Coastal Region. The district carries wards that may be named on a label: Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg and, since 2022, Piket-Bo-Berg. Darling, to the west, was a ward of the Swartland until 2003 and is now a district of its own with the ward of Groenekloof. A stated ward or district must be true for every grape; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. The Swartland Independent Producers' charter of 2010 is a private standard, signalled by a small seal, and has no legal force; it is nonetheless the rule book that defines the district's style.
tiers: WO Coastal Region
The region that holds the Swartland together with Stellenbosch, Paarl, Franschhoek, Darling, Wellington, Tulbagh and Cape Town; a blend across districts falls back to it.
WO Swartland
The district label, true for every grape in the bottle, and the one most Swartland wines carry.
WO wards
Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg and Piket-Bo-Berg: a ward names a single hill or valley and is used by the single-site wines.
Swartland Independent Producers
A voluntary charter from 2010: Swartland fruit only, native yeasts, no added acid or tannin, a limit on new oak; a seal on the bottle, not a tier of law.
Certified Heritage Vineyard
The Old Vine Project seal, from 2018, for a vineyard of thirty five years or more, with its planting date; much of the Swartland's old Chenin qualifies.
labels: Swartland
The district, meaning black land, after the renosterbos shrub that darkens after rain.
Paardeberg
Horse mountain, the granite dome on the Paarl border and a ward.
Porseleinberg
Porcelain mountain, the blue schist hill near Riebeek-Kasteel and a ward.
Kasteelberg
Castle mountain, the sandstone ridge above the Riebeek towns.
Koffieklip
Coffee stone, the iron-rich ferricrete gravel found in the district's soils.
Ou wingerd, old vine
A marketing phrase unless the Certified Heritage Vineyard seal and a planting date back it up.

places.name: Malmesbury
places.note: The district's main town and a ward in the shale country at its heart, home of the large co-operative cellar founded in 1948 that long absorbed the district's crop, and of the Sadie Family cellar on the Paardeberg side.

places.name: Paardeberg
places.note: The granite mountain in the south, shared with Paarl, whose Swartland face is the ward of Paardeberg with Paardeberg South beside it. Coarse decomposed granite, old bush-vine Chenin and Cinsaut, and the cellars that led the district's revival; its wines are perfumed, taut and mineral.

places.name: Paardeberg South
places.note: The ward on the southern flank of the mountain, warmer and more exposed, with the same granite and its own cluster of small cellars.

places.name: Riebeek-Kasteel and Riebeek West
places.note: Two villages under the Kasteelberg in the east of the district, the centre of the Swartland wine route, with Mullineux at Riebeek-Kasteel and the old estates at Riebeek West that once sent fortified wine and Shiraz to the whole country.

places.name: Riebeekberg
places.note: The ward on the Kasteelberg's slopes above the villages: shale and sandstone, cooler air with height, structured Syrah and Chenin.

places.name: Riebeeksrivier
places.note: The ward on the lower ground along the Riebeek stream, warmer and heavier in soil, with old bush vines on clay loam over shale.

places.name: Porseleinberg
places.note: A hill of hard blue schist near Riebeek-Kasteel and the ward named for it, where a Franschhoek house planted Syrah on the stones; its wine is the district's most famous single-site red, firm, graphite-edged and slow.

places.name: Piket-Bo-Berg
places.note: A ward gazetted in 2022, on the high plateau of the Piketberg in the district's north, with cooler nights and sandstone soils; its name means above the Piketberg.

places.name: Darling and Groenekloof
places.note: West of the Swartland towards the Atlantic, Darling was a Swartland ward until 2003 and is now its own district, with Groenekloof as its ward: cool sea breezes and sharp, green Sauvignon Blanc rather than the Swartland's reds.

places.name: St Helena Bay and the West Coast
places.note: The Berg River meets the Atlantic here at the district's north-western corner; a cool, windy coastal strip with a few vineyards, better known for the Benguela current's fishing than for wine.

producers.name: Sadie Family Wines
producers.why: The Malmesbury house whose Syrah-led Columella and white blend Palladius, from 2000 on, turned the Swartland from bulk land into a fine wine district.

producers.name: Mullineux
producers.why: The Riebeek-Kasteel house founded in 2007 whose single-soil Syrahs, Schist, Granite and Iron, teach the district's geology in three glasses.

producers.name: AA Badenhorst Family Wines
producers.why: A Paardeberg farm making textured white blends, Cinsaut and Grenache from old bush vines in old wood and concrete.

producers.name: Porseleinberg
producers.why: The schist-hill Syrah farmed by the Franschhoek house Boekenhoutskloof, the Swartland's single-site benchmark.

producers.name: Allesverloren
producers.why: The old Riebeek West estate, on a farm granted in 1704, that kept Shiraz and Cape port styles alive through the co-operative years.

producers.name: Lammershoek
producers.why: A Paardeberg estate whose old Chenin and Pinotage bush vines fed several of the revival's early wines.

producers.name: Swartland Winery
producers.why: The Malmesbury co-operative of 1948 that still bottles much of the district's volume and shows what the land made before the revival.

exam: Swartland against Stellenbosch: dry-farmed bush vines, Syrah and Rhône blends and old Chenin on granite and shale, against trellised Cabernet on the mountain slopes near False Bay.
Columella and Palladius by name: a Syrah-led red blend and a Chenin-led white blend from Sadie Family Wines at Malmesbury.
The two soils, granite on the Paardeberg and shale or schist around Riebeek and Porseleinberg, and what each does to Syrah.
The Swartland Independent Producers charter of 2010: Swartland fruit, native yeasts, no acid or tannin additions, little new oak; a seal, not a law.
The Old Vine Project seal: thirty five years, planting date on the label, from 2018.
The wards by name, Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg and Piket-Bo-Berg, and Darling as a separate district since 2003.
traps: Swartland is a district, not a region: it sits within the Coastal Region, and a blend of Swartland with Stellenbosch fruit falls back to Coastal Region or Western Cape.
Skurfberg, the famous old Chenin site, is in the Citrusdal Mountain district of the Olifants River, not in the Swartland, though Swartland houses bottle it.
The Paardeberg is shared: the Swartland side is the ward of that name, with Paardeberg South beside it, and the Paarl side is the ward of Voor Paardeberg.
Darling and Groenekloof are no longer Swartland; they have been a district and its ward since 2003.
The Swartland Independent Producers seal is a private charter; the only legal guarantees are the Wine of Origin seal's origin, vintage and variety.
Swartland Syrah is savoury and medium bodied; expect pepper and fynbos, not the jam and oak of a hot-climate Shiraz.

cards.f: Swartland: where it is and what it is
cards.b: A hot, dry district of the Coastal Region north of Cape Town, wheat country whose old dry-farmed bush vines make Syrah blends and Chenin Blanc. Towns: Malmesbury, Riebeek-Kasteel.

cards.f: Swartland's two soils and their landmarks
cards.b: Granite on the Paardeberg, perfumed and taut; Malmesbury shale and schist around Riebeek and Porseleinberg, deeper and savoury. Koffieklip gravel on both.

cards.f: Columella and Palladius: what they are
cards.b: Sadie Family Wines, Malmesbury. Columella: Syrah-led Rhône-style red blend, first 2000. Palladius: Chenin-led old-vine white blend. The wines that made the Swartland.
Voluntary, from 2010: Swartland fruit only, native yeasts, no added acid or tannin, a limit on new oak. A seal on the bottle, no legal force.
Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg, Piket-Bo-Berg (2022). Darling left in 2003 as its own district.
Schist, Granite and Iron: three Syrahs from Riebeek-Kasteel, each from one soil type, used to teach the district's geology.
Black land, after the renosterbos shrub that turns the hills dark after rain.

questions.q: Which Wine of Origin region holds the Swartland district?
questions.exp: The Swartland is a district of the Coastal Region beside Stellenbosch and Paarl. The Breede River Valley holds Robertson, the Cape South Coast holds Elgin and Walker Bay, and the Olifants River runs north of the Swartland.

questions.q: Which grape leads Columella, the Swartland's best-known red blend?
questions.exp: Columella is Syrah led, with Mourvèdre, Grenache and other Rhône grapes from dry-farmed bush vines. Pinotage and Cabernet are the Stellenbosch story; Cinsaut plays a supporting part in the district's lighter reds.

questions.q: Which granite mountain on the Paarl border gives its name to a Swartland ward?
questions.exp: The Paardeberg, horse mountain, is a dome of Cape granite whose Swartland face is the ward of Paardeberg, with Paardeberg South beside it; the Paarl face is Voor Paardeberg.

questions.q: Which rock underlies the Riebeek hills and the land around Malmesbury?
questions.exp: Malmesbury shale and its schist weather to iron-rich clay loams that give deeper, more savoury Syrah; the granite is the Paardeberg's. There is no limestone of note here, and the Cape has no volcanic basalt.

questions.q: Which watering regime is typical of the Swartland's old bush vines?
questions.exp: The old bush vines live on winter rain alone, their roots deep in the granite or shale, which keeps yields tiny and concentrates the fruit. Drip irrigation is common on newer trellised vines in warmer Cape districts; flood and sprinkler systems belong to bulk vineyards on the river flats.

questions.q: Which white blend from Sadie Family Wines is the partner of Columella?
questions.exp: Palladius is the Chenin-led white blend of old bush vines that Sadie Family Wines at Malmesbury makes beside the Syrah-led Columella; the pair, from 2000 on, made the Swartland's name. Both are named for Roman writers on farming.

questions.q: Which former Swartland ward became a district of its own in 2003?
questions.exp: Darling, towards the Atlantic, became a separate district with Groenekloof as its ward, known for cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc. Malmesbury, Riebeekberg and Porseleinberg remain wards within the Swartland.

regions.name: Stellenbosch
regions.summary: Stellenbosch is the Cape's fine wine capital: a university town founded in 1679, ringed by granite and sandstone mountains, fifteen kilometres from False Bay. It is a district of the Coastal Region with eight wards, and the exam wants three things from it. First, Cabernet Sauvignon and the Bordeaux blend, the district's signature on the mountain foot slopes. Second, Pinotage, crossed here in 1925 by the university's professor of viticulture and first sold by a Stellenbosch estate in 1961. Third, the cooling: the False Bay breeze and the Cape Doctor south-easter that keep a Mediterranean valley fresh. Kanonkop, Meerlust, Rustenberg, Vergelegen and Thelema are the houses to name, and the first Cap Classique was made here in 1971.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean, with wet winters and warm, dry summers, moderated by the sea. False Bay lies fifteen kilometres south of the town, and its breezes reach the Helderberg and the southern farms every afternoon; the Cape Doctor, the dry south-easter of summer, blows hard across the district, drying the canopy and holding off rot at the cost of some wind damage. Sites range from warm valley floors to cool upper slopes at 400 metres and more, so a single district holds early-picked Sauvignon Blanc and slow-ripening Cabernet.
terroir.soils: Decomposed granite on the foot slopes of the Simonsberg, the Helderberg and the Stellenbosch Mountain: a reddish, clay-bearing loam that holds water through the dry summer and gives the district's structured Cabernet. Table Mountain sandstone higher up, weathering to pale, hungry, sandy soils that suit white grapes. Malmesbury shale on the lower hills to the west, in the Bottelary and Devon Valley, giving softer, rounder reds. Alluvial sand and gravel along the Eerste River and towards False Bay.
terroir.topography: A bowl of valleys and hills between three mountains: the Simonsberg to the north, the Jonkershoek range and Stellenbosch Mountain to the east, the Helderberg to the south above Somerset West. The Bottelary hills and the Polkadraai hills roll westward towards the Cape Flats, lower and warmer. Aspect matters: much of the best Cabernet sits on south- and south-west-facing foot slopes, open to the afternoon sea breeze.
terroir.water: The Eerste River rises in the Jonkershoek valley and runs through the town to False Bay. The bay itself is the district's cooling engine, carrying Indian Ocean air inland each afternoon; the Atlantic, on the far side of the peninsula, matters less here than it does at Constantia and Darling.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The district's grape: cassis, cedar, graphite and a firm, dry tannin from the granite slopes, bottled alone or as the lead of a Bordeaux blend; ages ten to twenty years from the best farms.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The flesh in the Bordeaux blends and a soft varietal red from the warmer lower slopes.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Leaf, violet and perfume in the blends; a few houses bottle a serious varietal wine from it.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: Crossed here in 1925; from old bush vines it makes a dark, mulberry-and-smoke red of real structure, and it anchors the Cape Blend.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Full, spicy, dark-fruited Shiraz, riper than the Swartland's, strong on the Helderberg and in the Bottelary hills.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Old bush vines in the Bottelary and Helderberg give rich, textured, barrel-fermented Chenin, and the district has several of the grape's most serious houses.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy and green-figgy from the cooler upper slopes and the sea-facing farms towards Somerset West.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fine barrel-fermented wines from the Simonsberg and Banghoek heights, and the base of the district's Cap Classique.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: The Hermitage of the Pinotage cross; old vines survive and make pale, fragrant reds.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown mainly for Cap Classique, the first of which was made in the district in 1971.

wines.note: Deep, cassis-and-cedar reds with graphite, dried herb and a firm tannin that needs five years and rewards fifteen; decant, serve at cellar temperature, pair with beef, lamb or venison.

Cabernet Sauvignon led with Merlot and Cabernet Franc, sometimes Petit Verdot; the Cape's grandest red category, with Paul Sauer and Rubicon as its two benchmarks. Cigar box, cassis and a long, dry finish.
Mulberry, plum and smoke with a savoury, sometimes tarry grip from old bush vines; the best are fermented in open concrete vats and aged in oak. Serve with game, barbecue and spiced lamb.
A red blend built on Pinotage with Cabernet, Merlot or Shiraz; a trade category rather than a law, usually with Pinotage at between a third and two thirds of the blend.
Barrel-fermented, textured and dry, with quince, pear and honey over fresh acidity; the serious face of the Cape's most planted grape, good with pork, poultry and rich fish.
Pungent, flinty Sauvignon from the higher and cooler farms, and barrel-fermented Chardonnay from the Simonsberg and Banghoek; the whites a server pours most by the glass.
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, a category born here in 1971 and made by several of the district's estates.

made.viticulture: Stellenbosch is trellised country: vertical shoot positioning on wires, rows set to catch the south-easter, with the old bush vines of Chenin, Cinsaut and Pinotage kept where they survive, chiefly in the Bottelary hills and on the lower Simonsberg. The district has the Cape's best mix of altitude and aspect, and the serious Cabernet farms sit on the granite foot slopes of the Simonsberg, the Helderberg and the Jonkershoek range, facing the afternoon breeze. Irrigation is permitted and common on the lighter sandstone and alluvial soils, but the granite's clay carries dry-farmed vines through the summer on many of the older farms. The hazards are wind, which the Cape Doctor supplies in excess, and drought in the dry years; leafroll virus, which stalls ripening and dulls colour, was the district's chief vineyard problem for decades and drove a long programme of replanting with clean material. Harvest runs from late January for sparkling base and Sauvignon Blanc to April for Cabernet on the cooler slopes. The university, its research farm and the Elsenburg college keep the district at the centre of South African vine science, as they have since the Pinotage cross of 1925.
made.winemaking: The district's reds follow Bordeaux: destemmed fruit, controlled fermentation in stainless steel or in the open concrete kuipe that the oldest cellars still use with manual punch-downs, malolactic conversion in barrel, and 18 to 24 months in French oak, with a share of new wood that has fallen from the heavy regimes of the 1990s. The Bordeaux blends are assembled after a year in barrel and often hold back their best lots for a flagship. Pinotage is the exception that tests the winemaker: picked ripe and fermented hot and fast it throws the acetone and banana esters that gave the grape its bad name, so the serious houses ferment it cool in open vats, press early and use older oak, and some coffee-styled wines use heavy toast for a market taste. Chenin Blanc from old vines is pressed whole bunch and fermented in older barrels on its lees; Sauvignon Blanc is reductive and cold in steel. Cap Classique takes a second fermentation in bottle, with a minimum time on lees now set at twelve months, and the first was made in the district in 1971 from Chenin Blanc before Chardonnay and Pinot Noir took over.

law.classification: Stellenbosch is a Wine of Origin district within the Coastal Region, and the most used district name on Cape labels. It holds eight wards: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Jonkershoek Valley, Banghoek, Papegaaiberg, Devon Valley, Bottelary, Polkadraai Hills and Vlottenburg, the last gazetted in 2020. The Helderberg, the mountain above Somerset West that holds some of the district's best Cabernet, is an informal name, not a ward, so its wines say Stellenbosch. A stated district or ward must be true for every grape; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. Estate Wine means grown, made and bottled on one registered unit, and the district holds many of them. There is no classification of sites and no restriction on grapes; the district's producers have organised a collective around Cabernet Sauvignon, but it is a trade body with no legal standing.
tiers: WO Coastal Region
The region above the district; the fallback origin for a blend that crosses into Paarl, Franschhoek or the Swartland.
WO Stellenbosch
The district label, true for 100 per cent of the grapes, used by nearly every wine of the district including those from the Helderberg.
WO wards

Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Jonkershoek Valley, Banghoek, Papegaaiberg, Devon Valley, Bottelary, Polkadraai Hills and Vlottenburg (2020): a named locality within the district, used on single-site and estate wines.
Estate Wine
Grown, made and bottled on one registered unit; Stellenbosch is the district of estates, and the term appears on many of its labels.
Single vineyard
A registered block of one variety, six hectares or less, named on the label; several Simonsberg Cabernets and Bottelary Chenins carry one.
labels: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch
The ward on the Stellenbosch side of the Simonsberg; the Paarl side is Simonsberg-Paarl.
Helderberg
The mountain above Somerset West and an informal sub-region, not a ward.
Cape Blend
A Pinotage-based red blend; no legal definition.
Kuipe
Open concrete fermenters, still used by the oldest cellars for Pinotage and Cabernet.
Stellenbosch Kloof
A valley name on the western side, between the Polkadraai and Bottelary hills, used by a few estates.

places.name: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch
places.note: The ward on the south-facing foot slopes of the Simonsberg, north of the town: deep decomposed granite, cool afternoon air and the district's densest cluster of famous estates. Kanonkop, Rustenberg and Warwick are here, with Thelema above on the Helshoogte Pass, and it is the ward the exam asks about first.

places.name: Kanonkop's lower slopes
places.note: The farm whose Pinotage bush vines of 1953 and Cabernet-led Paul Sauer blend, first made in 1981, settle most Stellenbosch questions.

places.name: Jonkershoek Valley
places.note: A narrow, steep valley east of the town where the Eerste River rises, enclosed by the Jonkershoek mountains: wetter and cooler than the open district, granite and sandstone soils, and a small number of estates making long-lived Cabernet.

places.name: Banghoek
places.note: The high ground on the Helshoogte Pass between Stellenbosch and Franschhoek, above 350 metres, with sandstone and granite and cool nights; Chardonnay and Cabernet of unusual freshness.

places.name: Bottelary
places.note: The rolling hills west of the town on Malmesbury shale, warmer and more exposed to the south-easter: the district's reserve of old bush-vine Chenin Blanc and Pinotage, and of fuller Shiraz.

places.name: Devon Valley
places.note: A small, enclosed valley north-west of the town below the Bottelary hills, with shale and granite soils giving softer, earlier-drinking reds and some rich Chenin.

places.name: Papegaaiberg
places.note: Parrot mountain, the hill on the western edge of the town itself; a small ward whose name is rarely seen on a label because the farms below it use the district name.

places.name: Polkadraai Hills
places.note: The granite and sandstone hills south-west of the town towards the Cape Flats, open to the False Bay breeze: structured Bordeaux blends, Chenin and some of the district's organic and biodynamic farms.

places.name: Vlottenburg
places.note: A ward gazetted in 2020, on the low ground south of the town along the Eerste River between the Polkadraai hills and the Stellenbosch Kloof.

places.name: Helderberg and Somerset West
places.note: The south of the district: the Helderberg's granite slopes above Somerset West, within sight of False Bay, hold Vergelegen, founded in 1700, Rust en Vrede and a run of Cabernet and Shiraz farms. Helderberg is not a ward, so the labels read Stellenbosch.

places.name: Stellenbosch Kloof
places.note: A valley on the western side between the Polkadraai and Bottelary hills, cooler than its neighbours, with Chardonnay and Cabernet estates that use the name on their labels.

producers.name: Kanonkop
producers.why: The Simonsberg estate whose Pinotage from 1953 bush vines and Paul Sauer Bordeaux blend are the district's two reference reds.

producers.name: Meerlust
producers.why: A farm granted in 1693 in the south of the district near False Bay, whose Cabernet-led Rubicon, first made in 1980, was one of the Cape's first modern Bordeaux blends.

producers.name: Thelema Mountain Vineyards
producers.why: A high Simonsberg farm on the Helshoogte Pass known for a minty, long-lived Cabernet Sauvignon.

producers.name: Vergelegen
producers.why: The Somerset West estate founded in 1700 on the Helderberg, a byword for polished Bordeaux blends and for its historic gardens.

producers.name: Rustenberg
producers.why: A Simonsberg estate on a 1682 grant, known for single-vineyard Cabernet and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Simonsig
producers.why: The Simonsberg estate that made the Cape's first bottle-fermented sparkling wine, Kaapse Vonkel, in 1971.

producers.name: Rust en Vrede
producers.why: A Helderberg estate on a 1694 grant devoted to Cabernet and Shiraz and their blend.

producers.name: Warwick
producers.why: A Simonsberg estate whose Trilogy Bordeaux blend and Cabernet Franc are list regulars.

producers.name: Lanzerac
producers.why: The Jonkershoek estate that sold the first commercial Pinotage, the 1959 vintage released in 1961.

producers.name: Beyerskloof
producers.why: A Bottelary house that built its name on Pinotage alone, from everyday to reserve.

exam: Cabernet Sauvignon and the Bordeaux blend as the district's signature, with Paul Sauer and Rubicon as named benchmarks.
Pinotage: crossed at Stellenbosch in 1925, Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, first commercial bottling by Lanzerac from the 1959 vintage.
The cooling: False Bay fifteen kilometres south, the Cape Doctor south-easter, and altitude on the Simonsberg and Banghoek.
The soils: decomposed granite on the mountain foot slopes for Cabernet, sandstone higher up, Malmesbury shale in the Bottelary hills.
The wards: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch first, then Jonkershoek Valley, Banghoek, Bottelary, Devon Valley, Papegaaiberg, Polkadraai Hills, Vlottenburg; Helderberg is informal.
Stellenbosch against the Swartland: trellised Cabernet on mountain slopes near the sea, against dry-farmed bush-vine Syrah and Chenin in hot wheat country.
Cap Classique's birth at Simonsig in 1971, and Estate Wine as the label term the district uses most.
traps: The Simonsberg has two wards: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch on this side and Simonsberg-Paarl on the Paarl side.
Helderberg appears on wine lists and in conversation but is not a Wine of Origin ward; its wines are labelled Stellenbosch.
Pinotage's second parent is Cinsaut, then called Hermitage; it is not Syrah, whatever the Rhône hill suggests.
The first Pinotage was crossed in 1925 but not sold until 1961; the dates are thirty six years apart.
Cape Blend has no legal definition; the rule of thumb of a third to two thirds Pinotage is the trade's, not the law's.
Stellenbosch is a district, so a blend with Paarl fruit must drop to Coastal Region; the Western Cape on a label is the geographical unit, not a sign of lesser quality.
Vlottenburg is the eighth ward, from 2020; older lists give seven.

cards.f: Stellenbosch: the three things to hold
cards.b: Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends on granite foot slopes; Pinotage crossed here in 1925; False Bay breezes and the Cape Doctor keep a Mediterranean valley fresh.
Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Jonkershoek Valley, Banghoek, Papegaaiberg, Devon Valley, Bottelary, Polkadraai Hills, Vlottenburg (2020). Helderberg is informal.

cards.f: Paul Sauer and Rubicon: who makes them and what they are
cards.b: Paul Sauer: Kanonkop, Simonsberg, Cabernet-led Bordeaux blend, first 1981. Rubicon: Meerlust, near False Bay, Cabernet-led Bordeaux blend, first 1980.
1925 crossed at Stellenbosch; 1941 first wine at Elsenburg; 1959 the first commercial vintage, Lanzerac; 1961 released.

cards.f: Stellenbosch soils and what grows where
cards.b: Decomposed granite on the Simonsberg and Helderberg foot slopes: Cabernet. Sandstone higher: whites. Malmesbury shale in the Bottelary: old Chenin, Pinotage, Shiraz.
Kaapse Vonkel, made by Simonsig on the Simonsberg in 1971, at first from Chenin Blanc; now Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
False Bay, fifteen kilometres south, sends afternoon breezes; the Cape Doctor south-easter dries the canopy; the Simonsberg and Banghoek add altitude.

cards.f: Estate Wine on a Stellenbosch label
cards.b: Grapes grown, wine made and bottled on one registered production unit. Many Stellenbosch farms qualify and print the term.

questions.q: Which grape is the signature of Stellenbosch's granite foot slopes?
questions.exp: Stellenbosch is the Cape's Cabernet district, bottled alone or leading Bordeaux blends such as Paul Sauer and Rubicon. Sauvignon Blanc takes the cooler upper slopes, Pinot Noir belongs to the Hemel-en-Aarde, and Chenin grows everywhere.

questions.q: Which bay sends its afternoon breezes into the southern Stellenbosch vineyards?
questions.exp: False Bay lies fifteen kilometres south of the town and cools the Helderberg and the southern farms each afternoon; the Cape Doctor south-easter blows across it in summer.

questions.q: Which Stellenbosch ward holds Kanonkop, Rustenberg and Warwick?
questions.exp: The south-facing foot slopes of the Simonsberg, north of the town, carry the district's densest cluster of famous estates on deep decomposed granite. The Paarl side of the same mountain is a separate ward, Simonsberg-Paarl, so the suffix matters.

questions.q: Which estate released the first commercial Pinotage, from the 1959 vintage?
questions.exp: Lanzerac in the Jonkershoek valley sold the 1959 Pinotage in 1961. Kanonkop became the grape's standard-bearer later, Meerlust is known for Rubicon, and Simonsig for the first Cap Classique.

questions.q: In which year was Pinotage crossed at Stellenbosch?
questions.exp: The university's professor of viticulture crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut in 1925; the first wine was made at Elsenburg in 1941 and the first commercial bottling followed in 1961.

questions.q: Which name on a Stellenbosch wine list is an informal sub-region rather than a registered Wine of Origin ward?
questions.exp: The Helderberg, the mountain above Somerset West, holds Vergelegen and Rust en Vrede but has never been gazetted as a ward, so its wines are labelled Stellenbosch. Banghoek, Bottelary and Papegaaiberg are three of the district's eight wards.

questions.q: Which Stellenbosch house made the Cape's first bottle-fermented sparkling wine in 1971?
questions.exp: Simonsig's Kaapse Vonkel of 1971 began the category now called Cap Classique. Kanonkop is the Pinotage and Paul Sauer estate, Vergelegen and Rustenberg are known for Bordeaux-style reds.

questions.q: Which rock weathers into the reddish, clay-bearing soil of the Simonsberg foot slopes?
questions.exp: Cape granite weathers to a deep, water-holding loam that carries Cabernet through the dry summer. The Cape has no limestone of note in Stellenbosch, no slate vineyards and no volcanic basalt.

regions.name: Paarl
regions.summary: Paarl is the warm district north of Stellenbosch along the Berg River, named for the granite dome above the town that gleamed like a pearl after rain when Dutch explorers saw it in 1657. It was the seat of the KWV, the growers' co-operative founded here in 1918 that ran the industry for most of the twentieth century, and of Nederburg, the estate of 1791 known for its auction and botrytised Chenin. It is a Wine of Origin district of the Coastal Region, warmer and drier than Stellenbosch because the sea is further off; its grapes are Shiraz, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet, Pinotage and the Rhône whites. Franschhoek and Wellington were carved from it as districts in 2010 and 2012.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean and warm, a step hotter than Stellenbosch: the False Bay breeze loses strength by the time it reaches the Berg River valley, and the Du Toitskloof and Klein Drakenstein mountains to the east hold the heat in the afternoon. Summers are dry and bright, winters wet. The cooler corners are the upper Simonsberg slopes on the district's southern edge and the granite flanks of the Paardeberg to the west, where the Atlantic air arrives late in the day.
terroir.soils: Granite first: Paarl Mountain is one of the largest granite outcrops in the Cape, and its slopes, like the Simonsberg's and the Paardeberg's, weather to a reddish, clay-bearing loam good for Shiraz and Cabernet. Table Mountain sandstone on the higher ridges and the Klein Drakenstein, weathering to sand. Malmesbury shale on the lower country towards Agter-Paarl and the Swartland. Alluvial deposits along the Berg River on the valley floor, where the bigger volumes grow.
terroir.topography: The Berg River valley, running north from the Franschhoek and Drakenstein mountains past the town towards the Swartland, with Paarl Mountain on its western side and the Simonsberg closing the south. Vineyards climb the mountain slopes to around 400 metres and spread across the valley floor; the warmest sites are the low ground in the valley's middle, the best the slopes with afternoon shade or exposure to the west.
terroir.water: The Berg River is the district's spine, rising in the Franschhoek mountains and flowing north through Paarl and Wellington to the Atlantic. It supplies irrigation to the valley floor, and most Paarl vineyards are irrigated; the dry-farmed exceptions sit on the granite of the Paardeberg and the upper slopes.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The district's strongest red: full, dark, spicy and smoky from the granite slopes, riper and rounder than the Swartland's, often with Viognier or Mourvèdre in the blend.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: A great deal of it, from brisk dry whites and brandy base to old bush-vine wines and the botrytised dessert wine that Nederburg made famous.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe, plush Cabernet and Bordeaux blends from the Simonsberg-Paarl slopes, softer than Stellenbosch's and earlier to drink.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: Old bush vines on the Paardeberg and the valley slopes give rich, smoky wines and the base of Cape Blends.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot-scented whites and a seasoning for Shiraz, a district speciality since the 1990s.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Spicy reds and rosé from bush vines on the Paardeberg and Voor Paardeberg granite.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Full, barrel-fermented wines from the Simonsberg-Paarl slopes and a base for the district's Cap Classique.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Hanepoot and Muscat de Frontignan for the sweet and fortified wines of the KWV tradition, which the Boberg name still covers.

wines.note: Full-bodied, dark-fruited and smoky, with black pepper, liquorice and a ripe, round tannin; serve at cellar temperature with lamb, braised beef and anything from the grill.
Plush, cassis-rich reds from the Simonsberg-Paarl slopes, softer than their Stellenbosch neighbours and ready sooner.
From crisp, cheap and dry to serious old-vine wines fermented in oak; the district grows a great deal of the Cape's most planted grape.
Viognier, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne and Chenin from the Paardeberg side, waxy and aromatic, a house style of several Paarl cellars.
Botrytised Chenin Blanc, the dessert wine Nederburg pioneered with Edelkeur in 1969; apricot, honey and marmalade with sharp acidity, served cold with blue cheese or fruit tart.

wines.style: Fortified wines under the Boberg name
wines.note: Sweet Muscats, jerepigo and Cape port styles from the KWV tradition; Boberg is the Wine of Origin name reserved for fortified wine from the Paarl and Tulbagh country.
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, made by several of the district's larger houses.

made.viticulture: Paarl farms on a bigger scale than Stellenbosch and with more irrigation, because the Berg River runs through the valley and the summers are hotter. Trellised, drip-irrigated vines cover the valley floor and the lower slopes, giving the volumes that the KWV and the big brands were built on; bush vines persist on the Paardeberg and the older hillside farms, where Chenin, Pinotage and Cinsaut blocks of forty years and more qualify for the Old Vine Project's seal. Shiraz and Cabernet take the granite slopes of Paarl Mountain and the Simonsberg, Chenin and Chardonnay the cooler aspects. The hazards are heat and drought: ripening can outrun flavour in a hot February, so canopies are kept full for shade and picking is done at night or at first light. Harvest begins in January for sparkling base and finishes in late March. Wellington, to the north, is the nursery centre of the Cape, where most of the country's vine cuttings are grafted and raised, which made Paarl the source of the clean, virus-tested material that replanted the whole industry.
made.winemaking: The district's cellars range from the largest in the country to small granite-slope estates, and the winemaking follows the scale. Shiraz is destemmed, fermented warm for colour and depth, and aged in French and American oak, often with a little Viognier co-fermented in the Côte-Rôtie manner. The Bordeaux grapes follow the Stellenbosch recipe with a lighter hand on new wood. Chenin Blanc is made two ways: cold and reductive in steel for the everyday wine, or whole-bunch pressed and fermented in old barrels on the lees for the old-vine bottlings. The historic strengths are the sweet and fortified wines: botrytised Noble Late Harvest, which must be made from grapes with noble rot and carry high residual sugar, jerepigo from Hanepoot, fortified before fermentation starts, and Cape port styles from Portuguese varieties. Brandy distilled from Chenin and Colombard base wine in pot stills, aged at least three years in oak, is the other half of the KWV's inheritance, and Paarl remains a centre of Cape brandy.

law.classification: Paarl is a Wine of Origin district within the Coastal Region. Its wards are Simonsberg-Paarl, on the Paarl side of the mountain it shares with Stellenbosch, and Voor Paardeberg, on the Paarl face of the granite mountain it shares with the Swartland; Agter-Paarl is a newer ward on the shale country behind the mountain. Two former wards are now districts of their own: Franschhoek Valley since 2010 and Wellington since 2012. Boberg is a Wine of Origin region name used only for fortified wine from the Paarl and Tulbagh country. A stated district or ward must be true for every grape; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. Nothing in the scheme restricts the grapes or the style, so Paarl may bottle Shiraz, Chenin, Cap Classique and jerepigo under the same district name.
tiers: WO Coastal Region
The region above Paarl; the fallback for a blend that crosses into Stellenbosch, Franschhoek, Wellington or the Swartland.
WO Paarl
The district label, 100 per cent from the district, used by most of its wines.
WO wards
Simonsberg-Paarl, Voor Paardeberg and Agter-Paarl: named localities within the district for estate and single-site wines.
WO Boberg
A region name reserved for fortified wine from the Paarl and Tulbagh country; never seen on a table wine.
Former wards, now districts
Franschhoek Valley (2010) and Wellington (2012) were wards of Paarl and are now districts beside it in the Coastal Region.
labels: Simonsberg-Paarl
The ward on the Paarl side of the Simonsberg; the Stellenbosch side is Simonsberg-Stellenbosch.
Voor Paardeberg
The ward on the Paarl face of the Paardeberg, meaning in front of the Paardeberg.
Agter-Paarl
Behind Paarl, the shale country west of Paarl Mountain towards the Swartland.
Boberg
The fortified-only region of Paarl and Tulbagh.
Edelkeur
Noble choice, the name of Nederburg's botrytised Chenin Blanc, first made in 1969.
KWV
The co-operative founded at Paarl in 1918, now a company, whose brandy and fortified wines are its inheritance.

places.name: Paarl Mountain and the town
places.note: The granite dome above the town, named pearl mountain in 1657, with the KWV's cellars and the brandy tradition at its foot; its eastern and southern slopes carry Shiraz and Cabernet on decomposed granite.

places.name: Simonsberg-Paarl
places.note: The ward on the northern and eastern slopes of the Simonsberg, south of the town around Simondium, with deep granite soils and the district's best Cabernet, Chardonnay and Bordeaux blends; several of the Cape's grandest estates stand here.

places.name: Simondium
places.note: The village at the ward's centre on the road to Franschhoek, surrounded by the Simonsberg estates and on the old Boberg fortified wine country.

places.name: Voor Paardeberg
places.note: The ward on the Paarl face of the Paardeberg, north-west of the town, granite and gravel soils with old bush-vine Chenin and Pinotage and newer Shiraz, Grenache and Rhône whites; the Paarl mirror of the Swartland's revival.

places.name: Agter-Paarl
places.note: The lower shale country behind Paarl Mountain, warmer and flatter, with larger irrigated farms growing Chenin, Pinotage and Shiraz for the bigger brands.

places.name: Nederburg
places.note: The estate of 1791 on the eastern side of the valley whose auction, held since 1975, set the market for the Cape's rare wines, and whose Edelkeur of 1969 was the first South African botrytised dessert wine.

places.name: Wellington
places.note: The town and district north of Paarl under the Groenberg and the Hawequa mountains, a ward of Paarl until 2012: the Cape's vine nursery centre, warm Shiraz, Pinotage and Chenin, and a few old estates.

places.name: Tulbagh
places.note: The enclosed valley beyond the Wellington mountains, a district in its own right whose fortified wines share the Boberg name with Paarl.

producers.name: Nederburg
producers.why: The 1791 estate that gave the Cape its auction and its first botrytised Chenin, Edelkeur, in 1969.

producers.name: KWV
producers.why: The growers' co-operative founded at Paarl in 1918 that governed prices and quotas for seventy years and remains the name for Cape brandy and fortified wine.

producers.name: Fairview
producers.why: A Paarl Mountain farm known for Shiraz, Viognier and Rhône-style blends, and for the goat tower by its cheese dairy.

producers.name: Glen Carlou
producers.why: A Simonsberg-Paarl estate known for Chardonnay and Bordeaux blends on granite soils.

producers.name: Babylonstoren
producers.why: A Simonsberg-Paarl estate on a 1692 farm, famous for its gardens and for Chenin, Chardonnay and Shiraz.

producers.name: Plaisir de Merle
producers.why: A Simondium estate with Huguenot roots, known for Cabernet Sauvignon from the Simonsberg slopes.

producers.name: Perdeberg
producers.why: The co-operative at the Paardeberg's foot that bottles old bush-vine Chenin from the district's western farms.

Franschhoek Valley and Wellington as former wards, districts since 2010 and 2012.
Boberg as the fortified-only region name for the Paarl and Tulbagh country.

Voor Paardeberg is Paarl's ward on the Paardeberg; Paardeberg and Paardeberg South are the Swartland's.

cards.b: A warm district of the Coastal Region north of Stellenbosch on the Berg River; Shiraz and Chenin country; home of the KWV (1918) and Nederburg (1791).

cards.b: Simonsberg-Paarl (shared with Stellenbosch as Simonsberg-Stellenbosch), Voor Paardeberg (shared with the Swartland's Paardeberg), Agter-Paarl behind the town.

cards.f: Why Paarl is warmer than Stellenbosch
cards.b: It lies further from False Bay, so the sea breeze arrives weak, and the Du Toitskloof mountains hold the afternoon heat in the Berg River valley.

questions.q: Which growers' co-operative was founded at Paarl in 1918?
questions.exp: The KWV, the co-operative winegrowers' association, fixed minimum prices and later planting quotas, and built the Cape's fortified wine and brandy trade from its Paarl cellars.

questions.q: Which Wine of Origin name is reserved for fortified wine from the Paarl and Tulbagh country?
questions.exp: Boberg is a region name that appears only on fortified wine. The Coastal Region is Paarl's region for table wine, the Breede River Valley holds Robertson, and the Klein Karoo holds Calitzdorp's port styles.

questions.q: Which Paarl ward lies on the Paarl face of the granite mountain that Paarl shares with the Swartland?
questions.exp: Voor Paardeberg, in front of the Paardeberg, is Paarl's ward on the mountain it shares with the Swartland, whose own face carries the wards of Paardeberg and Paardeberg South; granite, old bush-vine Chenin and Pinotage on both sides.

questions.q: Which ward covers the Paarl slopes of the mountain that Paarl shares with Stellenbosch?
questions.exp: The Simonsberg carries two wards, one on each side: Simonsberg-Paarl on the northern slopes and Simonsberg-Stellenbosch on the southern, so the suffix decides. Voor Paardeberg faces the Swartland's mountain and Agter-Paarl lies behind Paarl Mountain.

questions.q: Which grape made Nederburg's Edelkeur, the Cape's first botrytised dessert wine, in 1969?
questions.exp: Edelkeur is botrytised Chenin Blanc, a Noble Late Harvest. Riesling and Sémillon are the botrytis grapes of Germany and Sauternes, and Muscat of Alexandria, Hanepoot, makes the Cape's fortified sweet wines.

questions.q: Which former ward of Paarl became a Wine of Origin district of its own in 2012?
questions.exp: Wellington, the vine nursery town north of Paarl under the Groenberg, was a Paarl ward until 2012; Franschhoek had left in 2010. Tulbagh is a district beyond the mountains, Malmesbury a Swartland ward, and Darling a district since 2003.

questions.q: Which river runs north through the Paarl district towards the Atlantic?
questions.exp: The Berg River rises in the Franschhoek mountains and flows through Paarl and Wellington to the sea. The Breede waters Robertson, the Eerste runs through Stellenbosch, and the Olifants runs north of the Swartland.

regions.name: Franschhoek
regions.summary: Franschhoek, the French corner, is the valley the Huguenot refugees settled from 1688, east of Stellenbosch and south-east of Paarl, closed on three sides by mountains. Its farms still carry the names of French villages, its restaurants made it the Cape's dining town, and its wine is varied rather than one thing: Sémillon from some of the Cape's oldest vines, Cabernet and Shiraz on the mountain slopes, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc on the cooler ground, and a concentration of bottle-fermented sparkling houses. It was a ward of Paarl until 2010, when it became the Franschhoek Valley district of the Coastal Region. Boekenhoutskloof is the house the exam knows, and the Berg River rises in its mountains.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean but cooler and wetter than Paarl: the valley sits higher, the Franschhoek mountains draw heavy winter rain, and the mountain walls shade the lower slopes for part of the day. Summer days are warm, nights cool, and the enclosed shape keeps the worst of the south-easter out while still letting cooler air drain down from the pass.
terroir.soils: Table Mountain sandstone on the high slopes, weathering to pale, acid, sandy soils; decomposed granite on the lower slopes of the Simonsberg and Groot Drakenstein side; deep alluvial sand and gravel on the valley floor, laid down by the Berg River and its streams, free draining and poor, which is where most of the old Sémillon stands.
terroir.topography: A narrow, flat-floored valley about ten kilometres long, running north-west from the Franschhoek Pass towards Groot Drakenstein and the Simonsberg, walled by the Franschhoek, Wemmershoek and Groot Drakenstein mountains, which rise above 1,500 metres. Vines take the floor at around 250 to 300 metres and climb the foot slopes to 500 metres and more; the pass end is coolest and the open end towards Paarl warmest.
terroir.water: The Berg River rises in the mountains above the valley and runs through it before turning north through Paarl; the Wemmershoek dam in the side valley supplies Cape Town. Rainfall is high for the Cape, so irrigation is lighter than in Paarl, though the sandy floor dries fast in summer.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: The valley's historic grape, Groendruif, with bush vines from the early twentieth century on the sandy floor: waxy, lanolin-scented whites of lime, beeswax and honey that age for a decade, alone or with Sauvignon Blanc.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Firm, cassis-and-cedar reds from the granite and sandstone slopes, the valley's best-known red beside Syrah.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Peppery, dark and fresh from the cooler slopes; the valley's best-known house built its name on Syrah, though its flagship Syrah now draws on Swartland fruit.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The base of the valley's Cap Classique and a barrel-fermented still wine from the higher, cooler farms.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy, fresh wines from the shaded lower slopes, and the partner of Sémillon in Bordeaux-style white blends.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown for the sparkling wines more than for still red, with Chardonnay in the classic proportion.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Present as everywhere in the Cape, with some old blocks, but behind Sémillon in the valley's story.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: A softening partner in the Bordeaux blends on the warmer farms towards Paarl.

wines.note: Lime, beeswax, straw and lanolin, dry and waxy, from bush vines that may be a century old, fermented and aged in old oak; a wine for roast chicken, pork and ripe cheese that gains honey and toast with ten years in bottle.

Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with a second fermentation in bottle and at least twelve months on lees, from a valley that calls itself the Cape's sparkling capital; brioche, apple and a fine bead, poured as an aperitif and with oysters.
Cassis, cedar and dried herb with firm tannin from the slopes; the valley's serious reds beside Syrah, served with lamb and beef.
Dark, peppery and fresh from the cooler mountain foot slopes, with whole-bunch lift and old oak; served with lamb, duck and peppered steak.
Bordeaux-style white blends, often barrel fermented, pairing Sémillon's wax and weight with Sauvignon's cut; the valley's answer to white Graves.

made.viticulture: Franschhoek is a valley of small farms, many of them old Huguenot grants, and the vineyard is mixed by design: trellised Cabernet, Syrah and Chardonnay on the mountain foot slopes, bush-vine Sémillon on the sandy floor, and sparkling base on the shaded, cooler ground near the pass. The old Sémillon is the valley's treasure: Groendruif was nine tenths of the Cape's vineyard in the 1820s, Franschhoek kept more of it than anywhere else, and bush vines planted early in the twentieth century still crop, some registered as Certified Heritage Vineyards with their planting dates on the label. Rain is plentiful, which brings its own hazards: downy mildew and botrytis in a wet spring, and vigour on the richer alluvial ground that must be checked by cover crops and canopy work. The mountain walls shade the lower slopes for part of the day, so ripening is slower and later than in Paarl, with Cabernet picked into April. Fire on the fynbos-covered mountains is the valley's other recurring hazard. Tourism shapes the farming too: the valley's farms are also restaurants, hotels and gardens, and the vineyard is kept to the sites that justify it.
made.winemaking: The valley's winemaking is as mixed as its grapes. Sémillon from old bush vines is whole-bunch pressed, fermented with its own yeast in old barrels and left on its lees for a year, with no new oak so the wax and lime show; the best is bottled on its own, the rest blended with Sauvignon Blanc in the white Bordeaux manner. Cabernet and Syrah follow the Stellenbosch and Swartland models respectively: destemmed Cabernet in small French oak, Syrah with whole bunches, gentle extraction and larger, older wood. Cap Classique is the valley's collective calling card, made by many of its cellars: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir picked early for acidity, a second fermentation in the bottle it is sold in, a minimum of twelve months on the lees under the current rule and often three years or more, then disgorging and a brut dosage. The valley's first Cap Classique, in the mid 1980s, came from a Huguenot-named house above the village, and the valley's route of sparkling houses is the district's identity to visitors.

law.classification: Franschhoek Valley is a Wine of Origin district within the Coastal Region, created in 2010 from what had been a ward of Paarl. The district name on a label is Franschhoek or Franschhoek Valley, and it must be true for every grape in the bottle; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. The district holds no registered wards, so the finer names a label carries, Groot Drakenstein, La Motte, Robertsvlei, are farm or locality names, not Wine of Origin terms. Boberg, the fortified-only region, historically covered this valley with Paarl and Tulbagh. Nothing in the scheme limits the grapes, which is why one district bottles Sémillon, Cabernet, Syrah and sparkling wine with equal right; the valley's sparkling houses belong to the national Cap Classique Producers Association, a trade body whose twelve-month lees minimum has since been written into the scheme's rules.
tiers: WO Coastal Region
The region above the district; the fallback for a blend that draws on Paarl or Stellenbosch fruit, which many Franschhoek cellars do.
WO Franschhoek Valley
The district, since 2010; 100 per cent of the grapes from the valley. Earlier labels read Paarl or Coastal Region.
Former ward of Paarl
Before 2010 Franschhoek was a ward within the Paarl district; the older books and older bottles reflect that.
Estate Wine
Grown, made and bottled on one registered unit; the valley's Huguenot farms use the term where they qualify.
Certified Heritage Vineyard
The Old Vine Project seal, from 2018, on the valley's old Sémillon and Chenin with their planting dates.
labels: Franschhoek
French corner, the valley named for the Huguenot settlers of 1688.
Groot Drakenstein
The locality at the valley's open end towards Paarl, under the Simonsberg; a farm district, not a ward.
Groendruif
Green grape, the old Cape name for Sémillon, the valley's historic variety.
Cap Classique
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine, the valley's collective speciality; MCC on older labels.
Huguenot
The French Protestant refugees who settled the valley from 1688 and named its farms.

places.name: The Franschhoek Pass end
places.note: The south-eastern head of the valley below the pass, coolest and wettest, where the Berg River gathers; sparkling base, Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon on the shaded lower slopes, and the oldest Huguenot farms around the village.

places.name: Groot Drakenstein and the Simonsberg side
places.note: The open, warmer end towards Paarl, under the Simonsberg and the Groot Drakenstein mountains, with granite soils and the valley's larger estates, including Boschendal, founded in 1685, and the Cabernet and Shiraz farms.

places.name: The valley floor
places.note: Deep alluvial sand along the Berg River where the old bush-vine Sémillon stands, some blocks dating from the early twentieth century; free draining, poor and the source of the valley's most distinctive white.

places.name: Wemmershoek
places.note: The side valley to the north-east under the Wemmershoek mountains, holding the dam that supplies Cape Town and a few high, cool vineyard sites.

places.name: Robertsvlei and the southern slopes
places.note: The folds of the Franschhoek mountains on the valley's southern side, higher and cooler, where Syrah and Sémillon are grown on the higher farms.

producers.name: Boekenhoutskloof
producers.why: The valley's benchmark house on a farm granted in 1776, revived in the 1990s, known for Syrah, Cabernet and old-vine Sémillon, and for its Swartland farm Porseleinberg.

producers.name: Boschendal
producers.why: The Groot Drakenstein estate founded in 1685, one of the Cape's oldest, known for Chardonnay, Shiraz and Cap Classique.

producers.name: Haute Cabrière
producers.why: The Huguenot-named house above the village that made the valley's first Cap Classique in the mid 1980s under the Pierre Jourdan label.

producers.name: La Motte
producers.why: A Huguenot-named farm of the late seventeenth century, known for Shiraz and Sauvignon Blanc and for its arts and gardens.

producers.name: Chamonix
producers.why: A high farm on the valley's northern slopes known for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir of unusual freshness.

producers.name: Le Lude
producers.why: A house devoted to Cap Classique alone, with long lees ageing in the Champagne manner.

producers.name: Grande Provence
producers.why: A Huguenot farm of 1694 at the valley's centre, known for Chardonnay and Bordeaux blends.

exam: Franschhoek as the Huguenot valley of 1688, French corner, with French farm names on the labels.
A district since 2010, formerly a ward of Paarl, within the Coastal Region, with no wards of its own.
Sémillon, Groendruif, as the valley's historic grape with some of the Cape's oldest vines.
Cap Classique as the valley's speciality, with the twelve-month lees minimum and the first valley bottling in the mid 1980s.
Boekenhoutskloof by name, for Syrah, Cabernet, Sémillon and the Swartland's Porseleinberg.
The map: east of Stellenbosch across the Helshoogte Pass, south-east of Paarl, the Berg River's source.
traps: Franschhoek is a district in its own right since 2010; an older note calling it a ward of Paarl is out of date.
The valley has no Wine of Origin wards; Groot Drakenstein and La Motte are localities and farms, not appellations.
Sémillon, not Chenin, is the valley's historic white; Groendruif means green grape and names Sémillon.
Boekenhoutskloof is a Franschhoek house, but its Porseleinberg Syrah is Wine of Origin Swartland.
The Franschhoek Pass is not the Helshoogte Pass: Helshoogte joins Stellenbosch to Franschhoek through Banghoek, the Franschhoek Pass climbs out of the valley's far end towards the Overberg.
Cap Classique is the Cape term; Méthode Cap Classique and MCC are the older forms of the same thing, never a different category.

cards.f: Franschhoek in the Wine of Origin scheme
cards.b: The Franschhoek Valley district of the Coastal Region since 2010; before that a ward of Paarl. It has no wards of its own.
Sémillon, the old Groendruif, once nine tenths of the Cape's vines; the valley keeps bush vines from the early twentieth century on its sandy floor.
The valley's collective speciality, made by many of its cellars; first valley bottling in the mid 1980s; at least twelve months on lees.
The valley's benchmark house, on a 1776 farm revived in the 1990s: Syrah, Cabernet, old-vine Sémillon, and the Swartland's Porseleinberg Syrah.

questions.q: Which refugees settled the Franschhoek valley from 1688 and gave it its name?
questions.exp: French Protestant Huguenots, fleeing after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, were settled by the Dutch East India Company in the valley that became the French corner. The Moravians founded mission stations elsewhere in the Cape.

questions.q: In which year did Franschhoek become a Wine of Origin district in its own right?
questions.exp: The Franschhoek Valley district was created in 2010 out of what had been a ward of Paarl; Wellington followed the same path in 2012.

questions.q: Which grape is Franschhoek's historic white, once known as Groendruif?
questions.exp: Groendruif, green grape, is Sémillon, which was nine tenths of the Cape's vines in the 1820s; Franschhoek kept old bush vines of it on its sandy valley floor. Chenin is the Cape's most planted grape but not the valley's story.

questions.q: Which Wine of Origin district was Franschhoek a ward of before 2010?
questions.exp: Franschhoek was a ward within Paarl until it was made a district; Stellenbosch lies west across the Helshoogte Pass, Wellington was itself a Paarl ward until 2012, and Tulbagh is a separate district beyond the mountains.

questions.q: Which Franschhoek house farms the Porseleinberg Syrah vineyard in the Swartland?
questions.exp: Boekenhoutskloof, on a farm granted in 1776 and revived in the 1990s, makes Syrah, Cabernet and old-vine Sémillon in Franschhoek and bought the schist Porseleinberg farm, whose Syrah carries Wine of Origin Swartland, not Franschhoek.

questions.q: Which river rises in the mountains above Franschhoek and flows north through Paarl?
questions.exp: The Berg River gathers in the Franschhoek mountains, crosses the valley and runs north through Paarl and Wellington to the Atlantic. The Eerste is Stellenbosch's river, the Breede waters Robertson, and the Palmiet drains Elgin.

questions.q: What is the current minimum time on lees for a Cap Classique?
questions.exp: The minimum rose from nine months to twelve, a rule the Cap Classique producers' association adopted first and the law then followed. Champagne asks twelve months on lees and fifteen months in all for a non-vintage wine, the figures candidates confuse it with.
